The Korean Wave–K-pop, K-beauty, K-entertainment, and K-food–has spread globally over the past two decades but, recently, it seems to have reached a crescendo. From Olive Young opening its first North American location in Pasadena, California, this summer to the frequently sold-out kimbap at my local Trader Joe’s, Korean culture is everywhere.

Global interest in visiting South Korea, not just appreciating its culture from afar, is driving traveler numbers to the country like never before—over 6 million visitors were recorded in the first quarter of 2026 alone. Some go to experience the splendor of the ancient palaces, tranquil Buddhist temples, and backdrops of their cherished K-dramas; others to try the street foods they’ve seen splashed across their social media feeds. And, as the popularity of K-beauty has spread, more and more travelers are flocking to South Korea in hope of achieving the glassy, glowing skin Instagram feeds are replete with. As a leader in aesthetic medicine offering top-notch treatments at a fraction of the cost as in the United States, Korea’s beauty tourism is booming—last year, 1.3 million visited for dermatology treatments and 233,000 for plastic surgery.

Anna Haines

This year, I was one of them. Well, sort of. I went to Korea to explore my father’s native country. But after six weeks of witnessing age-defying complexions, I figured when in Rome. I had scouted Seoul’s K-beauty scene back in 2024, but with the industry’s rapid development, I was due for a follow-up. After several clinic visits, treatments, and interviews with Seoul- and New York-based Korean experts—here’s what I wish I’d known earlier.
Choosing The Right Clinic

“Start by identifying your goals: do you want lasers, injectables, regenerative treatments, or surgery?” Dr. Eunice Park, the founder of AIREM, a medical aesthetic spa in New York, asked me. We had traveled to Seoul together in 2024 to check out the latest treatments for an annual K-beauty retreat she runs. I didn’t know what I wanted; all I knew was I wanted something.

For those who are unsure about the treatments they should be seeking, New York- and Seoul-based esthetician Erica Choi, the founder of Superegg skincare, recommends visiting a clinic known for a specialization. If you’re like me and need treatment guidance, a reputable clinic will tailor your treatment plan to your aging pattern, skin quality, and facial structure. Either way, avoid factory-style clinics offering one-size-fits-all packages at suspiciously low prices, advises Dr. Joon Lee at DOD Dermatology, where I had a combined radio-frequency microneedling and exosome treatment, designed to stimulate collagen and elastin production

Instead of following social media trends, prioritize the clinic’s credentials. Be careful not to mistake a non-medical ‘aesthetic spa’ for a dermatology clinic offering medical-grade treatments. “I recommend looking for clinics with ‘의원’ (uiwon) in their name, which indicates a licensed medical clinic—they often have a red medical insignia displayed,” advises Choi.
https://media.cntraveler.com/photos/6ab158fe9a0a85b128eb8710/master/w_1600%2Cc_limit/Anna%2520Haines%2520Beauty%2520Treatment%2520Seoul%25202024.jpg
blocks.c: Image may contain Adult Person Head and Face

blocks.x: Applying a soothing balm during a treatment session
Anna Haines

Similarly, ‘specialist’ isn’t the same as ‘dermatologist.’ While there are specialists skilled in aesthetic procedures, a dermatologist is more trustworthy, says Dr. Chang Sik Kim at Chang Dermatology. Every expert I spoke with emphasized checking that the dermatologist or surgeon has board certification, which indicates years of rigorous, specialized training.

Another green flag is transparency during your virtual or phone consultation. The clinic should communicate who will perform the treatment, any risks, and the expected downtime. Once you’re in Korea, request an in-person meeting with the physician performing your procedure. “Even if the clinic charges an upfront consultation fee, it’s the best investment you can make to ensure you get exactly what your unique facial anatomy needs,” advises Dr. Kwangyeol Lee, director of Diore Clinic.
Timing Treatments For Maximum Results and Minimal Downtime

Set yourself up for success by scheduling treatments strategically. Opting for minimally invasive treatments with less downtime afforded me the flexibility to explore the city and schedule treatments close together. “It used to be more pain, more gain, but now there can be less pain with more results,” says Dr. Shin Ji Yeoun at HEV Dermatology, where I had 10Therma, a lifting radiofrequency treatment that causes minimal swelling and redness.

If you’re getting more aggressive treatments like lasers, thread lifts, or skin boosters, experts recommend scheduling them early in your trip to allow time for follow-up appointments and any swelling, bruising, and redness to subside before flying home.

To maximize results and minimize downtime, take advantage of the Korean preference for stacking treatments. “The golden rule of sequencing is energy-based devices before injectables,” says Dr. Joon Lee. Combining certain treatments—like ultrasound and exosome skin boosters—can have a synergistic effect. “The ultrasound device stimulates deep collagen production, while the skin booster provides immediate hydration and accelerates the healing process,” explains Dr. Joon Lee. But stacking treatments should be planned carefully by your physician. Dr. Kim advises against getting more than one treatment that causes irritation and inflammation in the same day.

To reduce the cost of multiple treatments, Choi recommends asking the clinic if they offer bundled treatment pricing. But the esthetician advises against overbooking, “it can be tempting to try everything in one trip, but more isn't always better.”

Ask All the Questions

I learned the importance of asking questions the hard way. After five weeks of traveling the country, I had translation fatigue. So, when I didn’t recognize the name of the painkiller I received during a skin booster treatment, I didn’t press further. It was only later I found out how strong the painkiller was.
“If you don't fully understand, keep asking until you do,” advises Dr. Park. Before your treatment, find out what products and devices will be used, the recovery process, and potential complications.

All the clinics I visited had staff who knew basic English, but details were still lost in translation. “Google Translate or AI translation apps are fine for casual questions,” says Dr. Joon Lee. “But relying solely on an app to discuss personal goals, pain tolerance, and medical history can lead to subtle but important misunderstandings.”

Next time, I’ll arrange a translator. Dr. Joon Lee suggests checking the clinic’s website or Instagram to see if they have an in-house medical translator. If not, you can search for a certified medical tourism coordinator through the Korea Health Industry Development Institute (KHIDI). You can also ask the clinic to recommend a translator familiar with medical terminology to hire privately. “The cost of a translator is minimal compared to the cost of misunderstanding an important medical discussion,” says Dr. Park.
